transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-02-21 15:00 PT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Maya (Redwood SE), Riley, Samira, Carlos, Ava (Atlas Health)

Summary:
Quick internal/external hybrid enablement: map where conversational flows break in Atlas Health prototype, replay the demo sequences that caused failures, and align on pilot acceptance criteria and next steps. Walkthrough included one recorded demo clip + live replay.

Topics:
- Failure taxonomy (intent drift, context loss, hallucination, token limits)
- Hosting options: hosted API vs dedicated vs private VPC and tradeoffs for PHI
- Debugging transcripts and KV cache behavior
- Demo replay and remediation steps

-- Transcript start --
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for jumping on, I'm Jordan from Redwood, Maya's here who's going to do the deep dive on the replay. How's everyone doin'?
[00:06] Riley: Good, thanks. Excited to get into the failure cases, we've got a handful from our QA logs and some PM notes.
[00:12] Maya: Awesome. Quick note, I'm gonna share my screen and play a short clip from the recorded demo where the flow stutters at the handoff to the decision service. The clip is clipped at about 40 seconds.
[00:22] Jordan: Cool. Just for context, Atlas told us the failing case is around patient intake dialogs where follow-up questions aren't preserved, and you saw hallucinated medication suggestions, is that right, Riley?
[00:33] Riley: Yep. The most visible was that the assistant started recommending an OTC med that is contraindicated in pregnancy, and that made the PM nervous.
[00:40] Carlos: To add, the flow has a mid-conversation external lookup to our internal eligibility microservice. When that times out the assistant seems to lose context.
[00:49] Maya: Ok, that's helpful. I'm going to play the clip — you'll see the conversation, then the service call, then gap and the assistant replies with an unrelated rec.
[01:00] [clip plays — inaudible chunk, background hum]
[01:12] Maya: (after clip) Right there, you can see the KV cache doesn't rehydrate the prefix after the external call. There's a gap, then the model uses the earlier system prompt but not the recent user clarifier.
[01:24] Samira: When you say KV cache not rehydrate, is that the same as losing the session state or it's a token truncation?
[01:31] Maya: Good question — it's a bit of both in their setup. The sequence length was spiking because their prompts embed verbose patient notes inline, so token usage hit our configured hard limit on that instance and we fell back to a shorter context window. That plus the microservice timeout caused the cached keys to be evicted.
[01:48] Jordan: So shorthand: long prompts + external lookup latency = context window pressure -> eviction -> hallucination. Does that feel right?
[01:55] Samira: Yeah that matches our logs. We dump full transcripts for failed sessions, they show the user clarifier earlier, but it isn't present when the recommendation happens.
[02:05] Riley: Quick interjection — we also saw a case where the model used an older policy version. We were switching policies via an A/B header but the devs forgot to update the canary routing. Might be orthogonal.
[02:16] Maya: Totally — routing/version skew is another axis. We'll check both. For the context pressure issue, short term fixes: reduce inline notes (move to embeddings or vector DB), increase sequence limit on Dedicated or pick a model variant with larger context, or compress the system/user messages.
[02:31] Carlos: From an infra perspective, is there a noticeable latency/cost hit when we increase context length? We are very cost-sensitive.
[02:38] Jordan: There is. Token cost scales roughly linearly, and larger sequence models often run on bigger GPUs, so dedicated vs hosted choices matter — Dedicated gives more predictable throughput but costs commit. If you need private VPC for PHI, that also factors.
[02:53] Ava: PHI — yep we need a private option. Our compliance folks insist on customer-managed keys and VPC peering. Can Redwood support HSM/KMS integration?
[03:03] Maya: Yes, Redwood Private supports KMS/HSM integrations and audit logs. Our Private deployment can be air-gapped or VPC-peered and we can enforce key hierarchy. We'll share the security brief after.
[03:14] Jordan: And we can run a short benchmark for you in a private sandbox so you can see sequence length tradeoffs on your own data.
[03:20] Riley: That would be ideal. Also can we confirm the failure repro steps? I'll list the three top repro flows from our QA.
[03:27] Riley: 1) New patient intake, long notes pasted in 2) Eligibility lookup timeout 3) Policy canary mismatch mid-flow.
[03:35] Maya: Great — let's walk the second repro live. I'm going to simulate the eligibility microservice timeout by adding an artificial 600ms delay in the demo harness.
[03:43] [Maya shares screen, starts a live demo harness]
[03:50] Maya: Starting the flow now. User: "I was prescribed X and I'm pregnant, is X ok?" System: patient profile includes pregnancy flag. Then we call eligibility service, we delay, then you see the response.
[04:04] [live replay — assistant pauses, then replies with unrelated recomm.]
[04:12] Samira: There, again the assistant lost the clarifier. Can you show the token counts?
[04:17] Maya: Yep — here's the debug view: input tokens 4,600 — oh sorry 4,600 seems high because of the embedded clinical notes; model limit on this host was 5,120, so we're bumping close. After the external call the cache eviction policy frees the LRU keys.
[04:35] Jordan: Can we try a quick mitigation — compress the user clinical notes with a short extractive summary before append?
[04:40] Maya: Sure. I'll toggle the pipeline to summarize the notes down to the essentials; watch the token counts and the assistant's output.
[04:48] [Maya toggles, runs flow again]
[04:55] Maya: Now token footprint down to ~1,400, call delayed, assistant maintains context and answers correctly.
[05:04] Riley: Nice. So that's a concrete step: move from inline verbose notes to summary + embeddings.
[05:09] Samira: For long term we also want to analyze whether a model with 8k vs 32k context makes more sense vs changing our prompt patterns.
[05:17] Jordan: Right. We'll give you a cost sensitivity analysis: rough token unit cost increase for 32k model vs engineering effort to add summarization layer.
[05:25] Carlos: Another angle — can Redwood help with automatic fallback to a smaller summary-mode when the external service times out?
[05:31] Maya: Yes, we can implement a middleware that detects microservice timeout and signals a condensed prompt path — that's doable in their orchestration. We can prototype it in the sandbox.
[05:40] Ava: Tactically, our compliance wants full audit logs. Does the private deployment keep token-level traces?
[05:46] Maya: We keep structured logs and can optionally persist redacted token traces; we can also integrate with your SIEM. We'll send the logging schema.
[05:54] Riley: Quick note — there were also UX issues where the assistant interrupted users mid-sentence during the pause. Is that a model streaming config thing?
[06:01] Maya: Possibly streaming vs blocking. If you stream partial tokens without waiting for external lookups you'll get truncated outputs. We can change low-level streaming settings or hold output until the external call completes.
[06:12] Jordan: Ok that covers the repro and immediate mitigations. Next section — competitive positioning. Atlass noted ZephyrAI had an argument about integrated medical ontologies. We should be clear where Redwood differentiates. Maya do you want to lead?
[06:24] Maya: Sure. ZephyrAI focuses on verticalized ontologies and built-in domain rules. Redwood's angle is production-ready inference controls: predictable latency, transparent cost levers (batching, caching, quantization), and flexible deployment (hosted/dedicated/private) that works with your compliance needs.
[06:39] Samira: Zephyr's reps also sold them on "zero infra" which looks simpler, but the tradeoff is less control and higher chance of silent regressions.
[06:47] Maya: Exactly — we emphasize observability and rollback policies, like automatic fallback to a smaller model variant and per-route dashboards so you can see token usage per patient intake.
[06:56] Riley: Pricing is always the tricky bit. If dedicated private is required, how do we think about the pilot vs commit?
[07:03] Jordan: For pilots we can run a time-limited private sandbox and then present two paths: 1) extend hosted with stricter data handling for short term, 2) move to Dedicated or Private for scale and PHI. We'll price pilot separately and recommend a commit only after benchmark results.
[07:17] Carlos: I want to call out SSO/SCIM and RBAC — our enterprise needs role separation for triage and support staff.
[07:24] Maya: We support SSO, SCIM provisioning, RBAC and audit trails. We'll map the mapping matrix in the security doc.
[07:30] Jordan: Ok switching back to the demo, Maya — any other gotchas you noticed?
[07:34] Maya: One subtle thing: the model occasionally repeated system prompt content when the prefix was long; that was likely from duplication in the prompt builder. Small fix: dedupe system/user pairs before sending.
[07:45] Ava: That's useful. Also, on our side, we might reduce the verbosity of the system prompt to include only policy-critical lines.
[07:52] Riley: One more item — we saw a case where the assistant referenced patient name incorrectly — sometimes it used "Sam" instead of "Samantha". Could be NER mismatch.
[07:59] Maya: Could be our tokenization or embedding aliasing, or a preprocessing step that normalizes names. We'll add name normalization to the preprocessing pass in the sandbox.
[08:08] Jordan: Good. We're about halfway, want to triage the rest of the failing flows and then finish with an agreed pilot plan.
[08:14] [brief side chatter — scheduling]
[08:30] Riley: Ok next repro: policy canary mismatch. We had a route header switch and some sessions still went to older policy.
[08:38] Maya: That suggests routing cache TTL or an inconsistent lookup. If you're using a CDN or long-lived session affinity we need to flush or tag session-level routing. Also check your rollout windows.
[08:49] Samira: Engineering note: we were using a sticky session cookie due to legacy gateway, that could be the cause.
[08:55] Maya: Glue fix: include a routing key in the message metadata and enforce route on each request; don't rely on gateway affinity.
[09:03] Carlos: Regarding monitoring, can Redwood surface per-route model version so we can quickly identify skew?
[09:09] Maya: Yes, Redwood Console has per-route/model dashboards and traces that show which model/version served each request and token breakdown. We can set alerts on model-version mismatch rate.
[09:19] Riley: That would have saved us hours.
[09:22] Jordan: Alright final section: pilot acceptance criteria. Riley do you want to propose?
[09:28] Riley: Sure. 1) <5% critical hallucination rate on test prompt set, 2) latency p95 under 450ms for core intake route, 3) audit log retention 90 days, 4) security signoff from compliance.
[09:40] Samira: Add: deterministic fallback policy when external service times out.
[09:44] Maya: We'll add an automated condensed prompt fallback and test it in the sandbox.
[09:48] Jordan: We'll produce a short benchmarks doc that maps each of those criteria to metric thresholds and test harness steps.
[09:54] Carlos: Also include cost estimates for steady-state 10k sessions/day.
[09:57] Jordan: Good call. We'll add that.
[10:00] [wrap up planning, recap of next steps]
[10:12] Riley: Quick logistics — can we get the annotated recording? That clip was helpful.
[10:15] Jordan: Yes, I'll send an annotated recording and notes.
[10:18] Maya: I'll assemble the sandbox invite and a one-page remediation playbook.
[10:22] Samira: We'll collect the failing transcripts and token dumps and drop them into the shared drive.
[10:28] Jordan: Perfect. Anything else?
[10:33] Ava: Not from me. Thanks.
[10:35] Jordan: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the deck + benchmark plan.

-- End transcript --

Notes on quality: There are a few misheard words in the recording (clip noise), some technical terms transcribed as similar-sounding words ("KV cash" vs "KV cache" in some automatic segments). The transcript preserves filler words and a few overlaps.
